reason: This passage (2 Samuel 11-12) recounts King David's personal transgression with Bathsheba and his arrangement of Uriah the Hittite's death, followed by the prophet Nathan's confrontation and divine judgment. The narrative focuses exclusively on David's individual sin and its consequences through Nathan's rebuke and God's punishment. There is no account of the Hebrew people expressing complaint or discontent about their leaders. The only objections in the text come from Nathan the prophet (who confronts David) and briefly from David's servants (who are confused by David's behavior regarding his deceased child), neither of which constitutes a complaint from the people about their leadership.
